name: Saffire I–III
objective: Large-scale flame spread over fabric (Saffire-I and -III) and verification of oxygen flammability limits for several materials (Saffire-II), in uncrewed Cygnus vehicles in orbit.

fuel.geometry: Saffire-I/III: fabric card 0.4 m x 0.95 m. Saffire-II: strips 5 cm x 29 cm

hardware.facility: Cygnus cargo vehicle, free-flying after leaving the ISS
hardware.apparatus: Saffire module: flow duct + avionics bay (~53 x 90 x 133 cm)

pillars_basis: our classification (not an official NASA label)

test_variables.constant: Same flight unit; only the sample card and samples differ between the three flights. Thin-fuel tests at ~21% O2 and 100 kPa.
test_variables.varied: Sample type and scale (Saffire-I large fabric, Saffire-II several materials, Saffire-III same sample as I at a different flow).

notes: Test points cover only the four SIBAL tests listed in Table 2 of the Saffire IV/V paper; the Saffire-II PMMA/silicone/Nomex tests are not tabulated here.
Saffire-III flow: the 2016 slides say 'close to 30 cm/s' (plan); Table 2 lists 25 cm/s (flown).

name: Saffire IV–VI
objective: Flame spread and growth over thin and thick fuels in exploration atmospheres (reduced pressure, enriched oxygen) and the effect of the fire on the spacecraft: heat release, CO and CO2, smoke transport and detection, post-fire cleanup demonstration.

materials: Nomex (did not ignite in Saffire VI)
fuel.geometry: Samples 40-41 cm wide, 18-50 cm long, in a flow duct 30 cm high x 45 cm wide x 109 cm long

sensors: Thermocouples (6 remote CO2 + thermocouple sensors in the vehicle)
Inlet/outlet O2, CO2, CO sensors (outlet data usable only in Saffire VI)
Far Field Diagnostics: ionization detector and DustTrak particulate monitors, smoke cleanup unit

hardware.facility: Cygnus vehicle after leaving the ISS (Saffire IV on NG-13, May 2020; Saffire V on NG-14, Jan 2021)
hardware.apparatus: Saffire Flow Unit (SFU) + Far Field Diagnostics (FFD)

pillars_basis: our classification (not an official NASA label)

test_variables.constant: Flow 20 cm/s at the start of each test; igniter wires; same flow unit.
test_variables.varied: O2 22-31%, pressure 54-100 kPa, material / thickness / surface structure, flow direction (V-4 opposed), flow reduced to 5 cm/s in extinction tests.

key_findings.text: Fires of 1.5 to 3.2 kW in vehicles with 17-19 m3 free air volume; temperature rose only near the fire, while CO and CO2 rose significantly.
Both Saffire VI PMMA tests exceeded the 1-hour CO2 limit (3 mmHg): increases of 3.51 and 3.37 mmHg; CO levels were well above the 24-hour SMAC and close to the 1-hour level.
A 1 mg/m3 smoke alarm threshold was reached only at 981 s in test VI-3, after most of the hazardous gas release.
Thin fuels, higher O2 and heated fuel can keep burning without forced flow. Holding flow at 5 cm/s for 300 s before stopping it extinguished V-3 and V-4 immediately.
Thick PMMA flames in concurrent flow did not spread; flame length reached a limiting size (9.5 cm in IV-2, 11 cm in V-3 at 25.4% O2).
The normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 does not correspond to overall fire behavior in low gravity.

notes: Saffire VI paper is preliminary (its abstract says results for one test).
Saffire IV/V also discuss extinguishment strategy (reduced flow); we did not add Suppression as a pillar.

name: BASS-II
full_name: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
objective: Ignition, flame growth, spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flow in microgravity, to bridge the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 and real material flammability.

fuel.geometry: PMMA rods 6.35-12.7 mm dia, slabs 0.125-5 mm thick (1 or 2 cm wide), a 4 cm dia spherical section; fabric strips 1-2 cm wide

hardware.apparatus: Fan-driven flow duct 7.6 x 7.6 x 17 cm; O2 lowered by diluting the MSG volume with N2

pillars_basis: our classification; one PI objective also mentions suppression characteristics

test_variables.constant: Microgravity; ISS cabin ambient pressure (not stated numerically in the papers we read).
test_variables.varied: Ambient O2 (N2 dilution), forced flow speed and direction (opposed / concurrent), sample geometry and thickness.

key_findings.text: PMMA rod: steady spread at 13.6% O2 in BASS-II vs 16% O2 blow-off limit in normal gravity: negative oxygen margin of safety of 2.4% O2, so 1-g limits should be de-rated by at least that much.
key_findings.source: BASS-II_ASGSR-2014_poster.pdf, slide 'Spacecraft Materials Microgravity Research on Flammability'

key_findings.text: Heat release rates of most tests were well below 100 W; global equivalence ratio about 1.3 (fuel rich).
CO/CO2 ratios were about an order of magnitude above efficient flue gases (microgravity flames are not efficient).

notes: Pressure 14.7 psi is an ASSUMPTION (ISS cabin); the papers do not give a number.
Airflow: sensors paper says max ~55 cm/s; the 'Approach' slide says up to 40 cm/s.
O2 lower bound 13.6% is from the poster; the sensors paper says ~14%.

name: SAME / SAME-2
full_name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME-1 in 2007, SAME-2 reflight in 2010)
objective: Measure the particle size distribution of smoke from spacecraft materials heated below ignition, to design better smoke detectors. Uses three instruments (three size-distribution moments) plus TEM analysis.

materials: Dibutyl phthalate on a porous wick
fuel.geometry: Small samples heated by an electric wire in a smoke generation duct for about 60 s

sensors: Ionization chamber from a residential smoke detector (first moment)
ISS and Space Shuttle smoke detectors
TEM grids via thermal precipitator (analyzed after flight)

hardware.apparatus: Smoke generation duct, aging chamber (piston), diagnostics duct

pillars_basis: our classification (not an official NASA label)

test_variables.varied: Material, sample temperature, air flow past the sample (quiescent to 8 cm/s), smoke aging time (11-1800 s).

key_findings.text: Most average smoke particle sizes were 200-400 nm; quiescent (no-flow) cases sometimes gave much larger particles.

Very small Teflon and Kapton particles are hard for light-scattering detectors, while silicone and lamp-wick smoke is large; detection likely needs more than one moment of the size distribution to reject nuisance alarms.

notes: O2 and pressure are ASSUMED ISS cabin values; the paper does not state them.
The paper's abstract says five materials; its results list six (with DBP).
The challenge text says SAME-R; the paper calls the reflight SAME-2. Confirm the naming in PSI.

name: FLEX
objective: Map flammability limits of burning liquid fuel droplets and measure how diluting the atmosphere with CO2 or helium extinguishes the flame.
sensors: Video cameras (30 fps, some at 15 fps)
pillars_basis: our classification; the challenge text describes FLEX as the suppression (dilution) study

test_variables.constant: Droplet burning in the chamber atmosphere (airflow not stated in the table).
test_variables.varied: Fuel (methanol, heptane), pressure 0.69-3.05 atm, O2 0.12-0.34, diluent CO2 (up to 0.70) or He (up to 0.45), initial droplet size.

key_findings.text: 274 tests (2009-03-05 to 2011-12-08): 157 methanol, 117 heptane. Test end: 186 extinction, 61 disruption, 27 completion. CO2 and He were never mixed in the same test.
24 tests had O2 of 30-34%, all at 0.70-1.01 atm and without diluent; the lowest pressure among them is 10.33 psi, just above the 10.2 psi lunar limit.

data_quality: Test 114 has pressure = 0 (treated as missing, excluded from test_points).
Six tests (69, 75, 76, 79, 80, 81) have gas fractions summing to 0.98.
FLEX Identifier 193F001 is used by tests 70 and 73.
Missing or corrupted values: initial droplet diameter 12 tests, extinction diameter 77, burning rate 16, burn time 8 (two written as '~6' and '~9').
The FLEX report covers the first 284 tests; the table has 274.
Column units are incomplete in the CSV header ('Burning rate; mm'); take units from the FLEX report.
notes: Pressure converted from mmHg (x 0.0193368 psi).
Droplets (liquid fuel), not solid materials.

name: ACME BRE
objective: Materials flammability in still atmospheres as a function of material properties: extinction behavior, conditions for sustained combustion, and the relevance of existing flammability tests for low and partial gravity. A porous burner fed with gas simulates burning solids/liquids.

fuel.geometry: Flat porous burner; pure or nitrogen-diluted fuel

sensors: ACME insert: thermopile radiometers, PMTs (CH*, OH*), HD color camera (CH*, soot), intensified cameras (OH*, CH*)

hardware.apparatus: ACME chamber insert (~83 L free volume, constant volume)

pillars_basis: JASMAC paper: BRE is the ACME study focused on spacecraft fire prevention

test_variables.varied: Fuel (ethylene, methane), dilution, elevated O2 and reduced pressure (numbers not given in the paper).

key_findings.text: Flames burned for minutes at elevated O2 but self-extinguished at concentrations below about 25% O2; larger flames generally self-extinguished within 1.5 minutes, and methane flames within a minute.

notes: Test conditions are NOT in the paper: get them from the PSI table before this experiment can be ranked by conditions.
ISS operations: Jan-Apr 2019 and Jul 2020-Jan 2021 (Table 2).

name: ACME CFI-G
full_name: Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (ACME project)
objective: Observe non-premixed, quasi-steady spherical cool flames on porous burners (normal and inverse flames). Motivated by engine combustion; included here because it has the highest oxygen concentrations in PSI.

fuel.geometry: Spherical porous burner; inverse flames use up to 85% O2 flowing from the burner into a fuel-filled chamber

sensors: Intensified camera filtered for formaldehyde (cool flame) emission
ACME insert: PMTs, thermopile radiometers, HD color camera
pillars_basis: engine/combustion science; relevance to fire safety is indirect

test_variables.varied: Normal vs inverse flame, fuel (ethane, propane, n-butane), dilution.

key_findings.text: Cool flames were discovered in CFI-G testing with n-butane after the hot flame quenched by radiative heat loss.

notes: The 85% O2 maximum comes from the challenge text, not from a paper.
JASMAC says ACME is mainly focused on energy and environmental concerns; only BRE has a secondary fire-prevention emphasis.
ISS operations: Mar-Jun 2021 and from Jun 2021 (Table 2).

name: SPICE
objective: Laminar smoke points of coflowing gas diffusion flames in microgravity (sooting tendency of fuels).

fuel.geometry: Circular burners of 0.76, 1.6, 2.1 and 3.2 mm diameter in coflowing air

pillars_basis: our classification: smoke production informs detector design

test_variables.constant: Burning in air at atmospheric pressure.
test_variables.varied: Fuel, burner diameter, coflow velocity (3.0-47 cm/s).

key_findings.text: 57 new smoke points (112 in total) for methane, ethane, ethylene and propane; first laminar smoke point observed for methane at atmospheric pressure.
Sooting propensity ranked methane < ethane < ethylene < propane. Smoke-point length scales as burner diameter^-0.67 x coflow velocity^0.27.
In microgravity, higher coflow velocity or smaller burner diameter lengthened the smoke-point flame.

notes: Sensors not listed: the abstracts we read do not name them.
Naming: the challenge and the Dotson thesis write 'Smoke Point(s) In Coflow'; the JASMAC paper writes 'Soot Processes In Coflow'.
ntrs_reference: No NTRS record; UMD theses (drum.lib.umd.edu/handle/1903/13569 and /10005)

name: DAFT
full_name: Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test
objective: Risk-mitigation test of the P-Trak particle counter in long-duration microgravity in support of SAME; gave the first measurement of background particulate levels on the ISS (the cabin was found very clean).
sensors: P-Trak condensation nuclei counter (counts particles from 20 nm)
pillars_basis: our classification: supports smoke detector design

test_variables.varied: Not stated in the sources we read.

key_findings.text: First measurement of background smoke particulate levels on the ISS; levels were substantially below Space Shuttle and typical ground environments.

notes: The earlier version of this entry (lunar regolith simulant, ISO test dust) is not supported by any source we have.
DAFT-2: no source found yet. The challenge text says one SAME instrument was reused to detect dust in DAFT and DAFT-2.
